newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Shin Bet admits mistake on tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Shin Bet admits mistake on tunnel.

text.p: The head of Israel's Shin Bet secret police was quoted on Monday as saying his service had failed to predict the strength of clashes spurred by Israel's opening a tunnel in Jerusalem opposed by Palestinians.

Parliamentary opposition members called for a state commission of inquiry into the decision that triggered stone-throwing demonstrations and gun battles last week in which 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis were killed.
Shin Bet head Ami Ayalon made the comment at a meeting of the parliamentary Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee on Sunday night, Israel Radio said.
"He admitted the service made a mistake," the radio said. It said the Shin Bet was studying why its intelligence had been faulty.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, who was also at the meeting, told participants, who included opposition members, that he was informed of the tunnel's opening on the evening after Yom Kippur, a few hours before the opening took place, the radio said.
Mordechai last week questioned whether all factors were taken into account ahead of opening the tunnel.

Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, ended on Monday evening. Israeli municipal workmen punched a second entrance into the tunnel in Old Jerusalem's Moslem Quarter under cover of darkness before dawn on Tuesday.
Opposition members on the committee called for a state commission of inquiry.

"On things much less than this the State of Israel has established commissions of inquiry...I don't think there is any choice other than to establish a commission of inquiry," the head of the leftist Meretz party, Yossi Sarid, said.
Israeli Army Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Amnon Shahak told Israel radio last week that he too was only informed of the controversial step several hours before it took place.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he has no plans to close the controversial tunnel that touched off the clashes.

Israel's opening of the tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem, whose final status is a matter of hot dispute between Israelis and Arabs, combined with festering Palestinian frustration over Netanyahu's policies to ignite the gun battles.
